description: CSE student passionate about AI/ML, data analysis, and real-world problem solving. For NASA Space Apps Challenge, I’m exploring an AI-powered project combining weather, climate change, and agriculture to identify risks and support smarter agricultural decisions. Looking for motivated teammates with skills in AI/ML, data science, climate/agriculture, satellite data, UI/UX, web development, or storytelling.
summary:
AgriShift is a climate-resilient farm decision-support platform that brings NASA Earth data down to the level of a single field. A farmer draws their farm boundary on an interactive map, and AgriShift calculates the area and fetches daily NASA POWER data for that exact location: temperature, bias-corrected rainfall, humidity, wind and solar radiation.

The platform turns these numbers into simple risk indicators farmers can act on: heat stress, rainfall pattern, dry spells and humidity-driven disease pressure, shown with clear charts. Farms are saved, so each field can be checked again as the season changes. A prototype IoT dashboard shows how on-farm sensors for soil moisture, irrigation and weather will join the satellite data.

This addresses the Field Shift challenge by helping farmers adapt planting, watering and crop choices to a changing climate. It matters for Bangladesh, where millions of smallholders face rising heat, erratic monsoons and floods but rarely see scientific climate data. AgriShift makes NASA data local, visual and usable, and is designed to grow with SMAP, GPM IMERG and MODIS.
details:
What it does and how it works

AgriShift is a web platform that turns NASA climate data into farm-level decisions. The user draws the farm boundary on an interactive map. The backend validates the polygon, calculates its true area with geodesic maths, and saves it in a spatial database. For the farm’s centre point, AgriShift requests daily NASA POWER data (community AG): air temperature (T2M), bias-corrected rainfall (PRECTOTCORR), relative humidity (RH2M), wind speed (WS10M) and solar radiation (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN). Observations are stored per farm, and the dashboard shows:

  • summary cards and temperature and rainfall trend charts
  • four risk indicators: heat stress, rainfall pattern, dry spells and humidity-driven disease pressure

A prototype IoT dashboard shows how on-farm sensors will join the satellite data. It covers soil moisture, smart irrigation, a weather station, alerts and device management.

Benefits and intended impact

Farmers get scientific climate information for their own field, not a district average, in a simple visual form. Early warning of heat, dry spells and humid conditions helps them time sowing and irrigation and protect crops. Our first audience is Bangladesh’s smallholder farmers, who face rising heat, erratic monsoons and floods. The long-term goal is a single tool that combines NASA data, local agricultural knowledge and IoT sensors into a farm adaptation plan.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, GeoAlchemy2, Shapely, pyproj, httpx, Pydantic
  • Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, Leaflet with react-leaflet-draw, Recharts
  • Data: NASA POWER Daily API; OpenStreetMap base map
  • Hardware (planned): soil moisture, DHT22 weather, water flow, tank level and soil pH sensors, shown in the IoT prototype

Creativity

AgriShift starts from the farmer’s own field. A drawn polygon becomes the key for every NASA request, so global satellite-based data answers a very local question. Raw numbers are translated into plain risk levels with clear thresholds. The design connects satellite data with ground sensors, so one can check and back up the other.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: NASA POWER cells are about 50 km wide, so results are indicative. Risk thresholds are rules of thumb that need checking against BARC and BAMIS guidance.
  • Data latency: NASA daily data arrives a few days late, and missing values (-999) are handled without breaking the dashboard.
  • Usability: a simple map-first workflow for users with little technical background.
  • Cost: free, open NASA data with no API key, and open-source tools.
  • Roadmap: crop suitability, crop rotation, climate scenario simulation, soil inputs, and further NASA datasets (SMAP, GPM IMERG, MODIS, ECOSTRESS, NEX-GDDP-CMIP6).
